§ 2Content

§ 3ATMOSPHERE

  • The atmosphere is a mixture of gases surrounding Earth, held in place by Earth's gravity.

Evolution of the Atmosphere

  1. 1. Loss of Primordial Atmosphere: Initially composed of hydrogen and helium, however this atmosphere was lost due to excessive solar flares.
  2. 2. Volcanism: The hot interior of Earth release gases through volcanic eruptions to form a new atmosphere (Degassing).
  3. 3. Biological Modification: Plants and living organisms played a key role in further transforming the atmosphere through Photosynthesis.

§ 4DIFFERENT LAYERS OF ATMOSPHERE

Troposphere → (Tropos: Region of mixing)

  • Troposphere is the lowest layer of Earth's atmosphere.
  • All weather phenomena (rain, storms, clouds, etc.) occur in this layer.
Height variationComposition of Gases
At poles: 8 kmNitrogen (N₂): 78%
At equator: 18 km — Average: 13 kmOxygen (O₂): 21%
Carbon dioxide (CO₂): 0.036%
  • A tropopause is a line that separates Troposphere from Stratosphere.
  • As we move upwards in the atmosphere, the density of the air decreases, and that is why the densest air is found in Troposphere.

#### Temperature Behavior

  • Lapse rate is the rate at which temperature decreases with altitude in the atmosphere.

Standard Lapse Rate:

  • 165 meters → 1°C decrease
  • 1 km → 6.5°C decrease
  • Reason for temperature drop: The atmosphere does not heat up directly from solar radiation (insolation). Instead, the Earth's surface absorbs solar energy and then emits it as long-wave infrared radiation (Terrestrial Radiation), which warms the lower atmosphere. As the altitude increases, less terrestrial radiation is available, leading to drop in temperature.

#### Temperature at Tropopause

  • At Equator: -80°C
  • At Poles: -45°C

#### Effects of Insolation

  • At Equator: Insolation is less here, due to presence of clouds.
  • At Tropics: Insolation is maximum here due to minimal cloud covering. E.g. Desert.

Factors influencing Insolation include:

  1. 1. Transparency of the atmosphere
  2. 2. Length of the day
  3. 3. Earth's tilt and Rotation
  4. 4. Latitude
  5. 5. Altitude
  6. 6. Position of Earth
  7. 7. Surface reflection (Albedo)

Stratosphere (upto 50 km)

  • This layer of atmosphere contains the Ozone layer (30–35 km above Earth's surface), which protects from harmful UV rays.
  • While moving upwards, temperature increases with altitude.
  • Jet planes fly in this layer.
  • Stratopause divides Stratosphere and Mesosphere.
- Ozone Day is celebrated on 16 September to commemorate the adoption of the Montreal Protocol in 1987 in Montreal, Canada. This international agreement aimed to phase out Chlorofluorocarbons (CFCs) which deplete the ozone layer and contribute to the formation of the ozone hole.
- Ozone layer thickness is measured by Dobson unit.
- Kigali Amendment was made to phase out HFCs (Hydrofluorocarbons).

Mesosphere (upto 85 km)

  • It is the coldest layer of atmosphere.
  • Meteorites burn up and end in the mesosphere layer.
  • While moving upwards, temperature decreases with altitude.

Thermosphere (between 80–400 km)

  • It is the hottest layer of atmosphere.
  • While moving upwards, temperature increases with altitude.
  • It contains electrically charged particles known as ions, and hence, it is also known as the ionosphere.
  • Radio waves transmitted from the earth are reflected back to the earth by this layer.

Exosphere

  • It is the 5th and last layer of atmosphere. Mostly composed of Hydrogen and Helium.

Karman Line

  • It is an imaginary boundary located 100 kilometers (about 62 miles) above sea level that separates Earth's atmosphere from outer space.

Isotherm Line

  • These are lines or points on map/chart of the Earth's surface connecting points having same temperature at a given time.

§ 5Key Greenhouse Gases

  • Greenhouse gases keeps earth warm by trapping heat in the atmosphere.
  • Key greenhouse gases: Water vapor, CO₂, CH₄ (Methane), N₂O (Nitrous Oxide), O₃ (Ozone), SO₂ (Sulfur Dioxide).
Note: NO₂ is not a Greenhouse gas.

§ 6Heat Transfer Mechanism

  • The transfer of heat in the atmosphere occurs through three primary mechanisms: Conduction, Convection, and Advection.
  • Conduction: The process by which heat is transferred directly from one molecule to another without actual movement of air.
  • Convection: The vertical transfer of heat through the movement of air masses.
  • Advection: The horizontal transfer of heat due to the movement of air. E.g. Loo is a result of advection.

§ 7Albedo

  • Albedo refers to the proportion of incident light or radiation that is reflected by a surface.
  • Highest albedo is seen in ice caps or glaciers.

Albedo Values of Different Surfaces and Clouds

Earth surface(%)Clouds(%)
Oceans, Lakes8Shallow broken clouds (Cu, Cl, Cs, Cc)30, 35
Land Surfaces14–18St40
Sand, Desert27Thick clouds (Cs)74
Ice and SnowAc, As, Sc68
Sea ice35Cu75

Fresh snow80Cb90

§ 8Heat Budget

  • A heat budget is the balance between the heat that the Earth absorbs from the sun and the heat that it radiates back into space.
  • Of incoming solar radiation: 100% → 30% goes to Outer Space (reflected); 70% Rest gets reflected back → 23% gets absorbed by Clouds and Atmosphere.

§ 9Temperature Inversion

  • A phenomenon where temperature increases with height instead of decreasing.

Favourable Conditions for Temperature Inversion

  1. 1. Long winter night: During long nights, the Earth's surface loses heat rapidly through radiation, cooling the air near the surface.
  2. 2. Still air: Calm and stable air prevents the mixing of cold surface air with warmer air above, maintaining the inversion layer.
  3. 3. Clear cloudless sky: Clear skies enhance heat loss from the surface through terrestrial radiation, promoting rapid cooling and inversion formation.

§ 10Humidity

  • Humidity is the concentration of water vapour present in the air.

Types

  1. 1. Absolute Humidity: It is the total mass of water vapor present in a unit volume of air at a given temperature.
  2. 2. Relative Humidity: Actual moisture percentage compared to maximum capacity.
Absolute humidity is higher in warm air compared to cold air. This is because warm air can hold more water vapor due to its higher energy level.

§ 11Water Cycle

  • Water cycle is the continuous movement of water between the Earth's atmosphere and surface.

Evaporation

  • Evaporation is a process in the water cycle that changes liquid water into water vapour.

Precipitation

  • Precipitation is any liquid or frozen water that forms in the atmosphere and falls back to the earth in the form of rain, snow or hail.

Types of Precipitation

  1. 1. Rain: Liquid water droplet that fall when the air temperature is above freezing point.
  2. 2. Snow: Frozen water crystals that are formed when temperature is below freezing point.
  3. 3. Sleet: Small pallets of ice that forms when raindrops freeze before reaching the surface.
  4. 4. Hail: It is a type of precipitation that falls to the ground in the form of ice balls or lumps.

§ 12WATER ON EARTH

  • 97.2% of Earth's water is saline; only 2.8% is freshwater.
  • Out of 2.8% freshwater: Ice caps/glaciers (2%), Groundwater (0.68%), Lakes (0.4%), Atmosphere, River.
  • As a whole (Freshwater): Ice caps/glaciers (68.7%), groundwater (30.1%).
- 71% of Earth's surface covered with water
- 29% of Earth's surface is covered with land

§ 13Condensation

  • It is the process where water vapour (gas) becomes water (liquid).

Different Forms

  • Dew: It is the moisture that form as a result of condensation.
  • Fog: It is the thick clouds that forms close to the ground and reduce visibility. In fog the size of water droplets tend to be larger compared to those in mist.
  • Mist: Mist is a phenomenon caused by small droplets of water suspended in the cold air, usually by condensation. Mist contains more moisture than fog. In fog and mist, water vapor condenses around hygroscopic particles (aerosols like dust and smoke particles) instead of requiring a solid surface.
  • Frost: It forms when water vapor (gas) directly turns into solid ice crystals without becoming liquid first.
  • Clouds
Smog: Smog is a type of air pollution that results from the combination of smoke and fog.

Dew Point

  • The dew point is the temperature at which air becomes fully saturated with moisture, causing water vapor to condense into liquid droplets.
  • In winter air cools down due to which dew point reduces, water vapour condenses into water.

§ 14CLOUDS

  • Clouds are visible masses of tiny water droplets or ice crystals suspended in the Earth's atmosphere.
Isoneph: Line drawn on map, connecting the points containing same amount of clouds.

Different Types of Clouds

CloudsFeaturesHeight
NimbusRain bearing; Opaque; GreyLow-level
StratusLayered cloudsLow-level
CumulusWool / Cauliflower shaped; flat base4000–7000 m (Middle level)
CirrusFeather shape clouds, do not cause rain8000–12000 m (High altitude)
CumulonimbusProduce severe weather that contribute to cyclonesExtensive vertical development

§ 15Rainfall

  • Rainfall is the amount of water that falls from the atmosphere as precipitation over a specific period and area.

Types of Rainfall

  • Convectional Rainfall: It occurs when the surface of earth is heated up by the Sun.
  • Orographic Rainfall: Precipitation that occurs when moist air is forced to rise over a mountain range.

Windward and Leeward Side of Orographic Rainfall:

  1. 1. Windward Side (wet side): This side of the mountain facing the wind (mostly affected by Anabatic wind) receives the heavy rainfall as the air rises and cools there. E.g. Western Ghats.
  2. 2. Leeward Side (dry side): This side of the mountain faces away from the wind (mostly affected by Katabatic wind) receives less rainfall because the air loses its moisture on the windward side before descending dry. It is also called a rain-shadow region. E.g. Leeward side of Western Ghats.
  • Frontal/Cyclonic Rainfall: It is a type of precipitation that occurs when warm, moist air meets cold, dry air mass.

§ 16Key concepts

  • Atmosphere = mixture of gases surrounding Earth, held by gravity.
  • Evolution: Loss of primordial atmosphere (H/He lost via solar flares) → Volcanism (degassing) → Biological modification (photosynthesis).
  • Layers (bottom → top): Troposphere, Stratosphere, Mesosphere, Thermosphere, Exosphere.
  • Troposphere — lowest; all weather; average 13 km (8 km poles, 18 km equator); densest. Tropopause separates it from Stratosphere. N₂ 78%, O₂ 21%, Ar 0.9%, CO₂ 0.036%.
  • Lapse rate = rate of temperature decrease with altitude. Standard: 165 m → 1°C drop; 1 km → 6.5°C drop. Earth absorbs solar energy, emits as long-wave infrared (Terrestrial Radiation) that warms the lower atmosphere; less terrestrial radiation at higher altitude → temperature drops. Tropopause temp: Equator -80°C, Poles -45°C.
  • Insolation at Equator is less (due to clouds); at Tropics is max (e.g. Desert). Factors: transparency, day length, Earth's tilt/rotation, latitude, altitude, position, surface reflection (Albedo).
  • Stratosphere (up to 50 km) — Ozone layer at 30–35 km (protects from UV). Temperature increases with altitude. Jet planes fly here. Stratopause divides Stratosphere and Mesosphere. Ozone Day = 16 September; Montreal Protocol (1987, Montreal, Canada) phase out CFCs; Dobson unit measures ozone thickness; Kigali Amendment phase out HFCs.
  • Mesosphere (up to 85 km) — coldest layer; meteorites burn up here; temperature decreases with altitude.
  • Thermosphere (80–400 km) — hottest; temperature increases with altitude; charged particles = ions → Ionosphere; reflects radio waves.
  • Exosphere — 5th/last layer; mostly H + He.
  • Karman Line = 100 km above sea level, separates atmosphere from outer space.
  • Isotherm Line = lines/points connecting places with same temperature at a given time.
  • Key greenhouse gases: Water vapor, CO₂, CH₄ (Methane), N₂O (Nitrous Oxide), O₃ (Ozone), SO₂ (Sulfur Dioxide). NO₂ is not a greenhouse gas.
  • Heat Transfer: Conduction (molecule to molecule, no air movement), Convection (vertical, air mass movement), Advection (horizontal, air movement; e.g. Loo).
  • Albedo = proportion of incident light/radiation reflected by a surface. Highest in ice caps/glaciers. Values: Ocean/Lakes 8%, Land 14–18%, Sand/Desert 27%, Sea ice 35%, Old snow 59%, Fresh snow 80%. Cloud albedo: shallow broken (Cu, Cl, Cs, Cc) 30–35, St 40, thick Cs 74, Ac/As/Sc 68, Cu 75, Ns 85, Cb 90.
  • Heat Budget = balance between incoming and outgoing Earth radiation. 30% reflected to space, 70% absorbed (23% by clouds + atmosphere).
  • Temperature Inversion = temperature increases with height instead of decreasing. Favourable: long winter night, still air, clear cloudless sky.
  • Humidity = concentration of water vapour in air. Absolute humidity = total mass of water vapor in unit volume of air at a given temperature. Relative humidity = actual moisture % vs maximum capacity. Warm air holds more water vapor (higher energy).
  • Water cycle = continuous movement of water between atmosphere and surface. Stages: Evaporation (liquid → water vapour) → Condensation → Precipitation → Collection.
  • Precipitation = liquid or frozen water falling as rain, snow or hail. Types: Rain (liquid, temp > freezing), Snow (frozen crystals, temp < freezing), Sleet (small ice pallets from raindrops freezing before surface), Hail (ice balls/lumps).
  • Water on Earth: 97.2% saline, 2.8% freshwater. Of 2.8%: Ice caps/glaciers 2%, Groundwater 0.68%, Lakes 0.4%, Atmosphere, River. Of freshwater: Ice caps/glaciers 68.7%, Groundwater 30.1%. 71% of Earth's surface = water, 29% = land.
  • Condensation = water vapour (gas) → water (liquid). Forms: Dew (moisture from condensation), Fog (thick clouds near ground, larger droplets than mist), Mist (small droplets in cold air, more moisture than fog; forms around hygroscopic particles like dust/smoke), Frost (water vapor directly → solid ice crystals, no liquid phase), Clouds.
  • Smog = smoke + fog (air pollution).
  • Dew Point = temperature at which air becomes fully saturated; water vapor condenses into liquid droplets. In winter, lower dew point → water vapour condenses.
  • Clouds = visible masses of water droplets/ice crystals. Isoneph = line connecting points with same cloud amount.
  • Cloud types: Nimbus (rain-bearing, opaque, grey, low-level), Stratus (layered, low-level), Cumulus (wool/cauliflower, flat base, 4000–7000 m, middle), Cirrus (feather-shaped, no rain, 8000–12000 m, high altitude), Cumulonimbus (severe weather, cyclones, extensive vertical development).
  • Rainfall = water falling from atmosphere as precipitation. Types:
  • Convectional — surface heated by sun.
  • Orographic — moist air forced up a mountain.
  • Windward Side (wet) — faces wind, Anabatic wind, heavy rainfall. E.g. Western Ghats.
  • Leeward Side (dry) — faces away, Katabatic wind, less rain, rain-shadow region. E.g. Leeward side of Western Ghats.
  • Frontal/Cyclonic — warm moist air meets cold dry air mass.
